abstract: The unique flavor of dry-cured ham has been described as "savor cached in the bone". Herein, ham was spatially stratified into skin, adipose, muscle, and bone layers to investigate the contribution of bone, with emphasis on substrate composition as a key determinant of the spatial distribution of taste compounds and microbiota. Sensory evaluation and non-volatile metabolomics revealed that eight metabolites significantly contributed to the characteristic aftertaste of the bone layer. Microbiome profiling and correlation analysis identified Mortierella sp. as a key microorganism strongly associated with these metabolites. Further in vitro fermentation experiments showed that Mortierella sp. significantly increased four of the eight core metabolites. Microstructural and textural analyses revealed that fermentation induced degradation of bone matrix, facilitating the internal migration of these metabolites. This study advancing the fundamental understanding of flavor formation in dry-cured ham, offering practical strategies to enhance product quality through process optimization.
